metaTitle: AI assistant for Chrome on Mac: ask about any page, out loud
description: Lazur is an AI assistant for Chrome on Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about the page, hear the answer, and get guided clicks in Chrome settings.

intro: Lazur is an AI assistant for Chrome on Mac. It is a Mac app that works alongside Chrome, not a Chrome extension, so you hold a key, ask a question, and hear the answer out loud. It can circle things on the page, guide you through settings one click at a time, and type text where your cursor sits.
tldr: Hold ⌥⌘ in Chrome to ask about what is on screen. Lazur answers out loud.
Ask where something is and Lazur circles it. Ask how to do something and it guides you one click at a time.
Hold fn to dictate into any text box. Ask Lazur to draft a reply and it types the text at your cursor.
Chrome on Mac needs macOS 13 Ventura or later, according to Google. Check your Chrome version on the About Google Chrome page.
Lazur does not click for you. You stay in control of every click and every message you send.

blocks.text: Lazur lives on your Mac, not inside your browser. You install it once, then hold the shortcut from any window, Chrome included. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for Chrome or any other app. That matters for what you can expect. Chrome has its own AI features, such as Gemini in Chrome, which Google lists on its Chrome page. Those work inside the browser. Lazur works across your apps, so the same question works in Chrome, in Mail, or in a PDF open in Preview.
What to say to Lazur while you use Chrome

You do not need special commands. Talk the way you would to a colleague sitting beside you. Hold ⌥⌘, ask, and let go. Lazur looks at the screen only while the key is down. The answer comes back out loud. Most requests fall into five kinds, and each kind gets a different kind of help.

items: Explain: ask 'What does this error mean?' Lazur reads what is on screen and answers out loud.
Point: ask 'Where is the bookmark button?' Lazur draws a circle and a label around it.
Guide: ask 'Walk me through clearing my history.' Lazur names one click, then waits for you.
Draft: ask 'Draft a short reply to this email.' Lazur writes the text and types it at your cursor.
Dictate: hold fn and speak. Your words appear as formatted text at the cursor.

blocks.text: Ask Lazur to explain what is on the page

Explain fits the moment a page makes no sense. Say a tab shows 'This site can't be reached.' Hold ⌥⌘ and ask what it means. Lazur reads the message, names likely causes such as a mistyped address or a dropped connection, and suggests what to check first. It does not fix anything on its own. You choose the next step.

Explain works on what is visible when you hold the key. If a long article has the answer near the bottom, scroll there first. Then ask. Lazur answers from the screen as it looks at that moment. A question about a paragraph three screens up needs that paragraph on screen.

Explain also helps with a page full of unfamiliar terms. A cookie banner, a checkout form, or a settings panel can hide a choice you did not mean to make. Ask what each option does before you click anything. Read the answer, then decide.

Test the answers on things you can check. Ask about something you already know, and see how close the reply comes. Use the same habit for prices, dates, and version numbers. Those change often, so confirm them on the source page before you act.
Point at a button, menu, or setting in Chrome on Mac

Point is for when you know the goal but not the place. Ask 'where is' followed by the thing you want. Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. You move the pointer and click yourself. Point helps most when Chrome hides an option behind a small icon or a menu you have not opened before.
Chrome on Mac also has a keyboard for most common moves. Google's official shortcut page lists the ones below. Learn two or three of them, and you will need fewer pointing requests.

items: ⌘T opens a new tab. ⌘W closes the current tab.
⌘⇧T reopens the tab you closed last.
⌘L jumps to the address bar.
⌘⌥I opens Developer Tools.
⌘⇧N opens an Incognito window.
Fn+F turns on full screen, according to Google. Some third-party guides give ⌘⌃F instead, so test both on your keyboard.

blocks.text: Pointing works best with a specific name. 'Where is the thing' gets a vague circle. 'Where is the Incognito option in the three-dot menu' gives Lazur more to go on. Name the menu, the icon, or the corner you can see.
Pointing fails when a pop-up covers the target or when the menu you need is closed. Close the pop-up, open the menu, then hold ⌥⌘ again.
Walk through a Chrome feature one click at a time

Guide is the mode for work with several steps. Lazur names the first click, circles it, and waits. You click. Then Lazur names the next step. This is slower than doing it alone. For settings, that is the point, because one wrong click can change more than you meant.

items: Hold ⌥⌘ and say what you want, for example 'Walk me through turning on Memory Saver.'
Lazur names the first click and circles the target on screen.
You click. Lazur waits for that click before it names the next one.
Repeat until the setting is on, then check the result on screen.

blocks.text: Memory Saver makes a good first example. Google's Chrome page says the feature can reduce memory use by up to 148 MB. Google's speed guide also suggests closing unused tabs with ⌘W, turning off extensions you do not use, and ending heavy tasks in Task Manager. It lists Preload pages under Settings > Performance. Ask Lazur to walk you through each one.

Use guide when you have to think about where to click. Skip it when you already know the menu. A quick check: if you can name the setting, click it yourself. If you cannot, ask for a walkthrough. Guide also helps when a setting uses unfamiliar words, because Lazur can explain the option before you change it.
Draft text at your cursor and dictate with fn

Draft and dictate solve two different problems. Dictation turns your speech into text. Draft means Lazur writes the words for you. In both cases the text lands at your cursor in whatever box Chrome has open. That can be a search field, a comment box, or a form.

To dictate, click into the box first so the cursor blinks there. Hold fn and speak. Let go when you finish. Your words appear as clean text with punctuation. Lazur also supports snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots. Add names and terms you type often to the dictionary once, so they come out the way you want.

Say an email is open in Chrome and you need a short reply. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask: 'Draft a short reply that says Thursday works and asks for the agenda.' Lazur writes the reply and types it at your cursor. Read it before you send. Lazur does not press send for you.

Do not dictate passwords, card numbers, or other secrets. Store logins in Google Password Manager, which has its own help topic in Chrome. Dictation is for sentences, not for codes you must type exactly.
Chrome on Mac requirements and checking your version

Chrome on Mac needs macOS 13 Ventura or later, according to Google's download page. Chrome on an older macOS is not supported. Choose Apple menu > About This Mac to see your version. Lazur runs on Macs with Apple silicon or Intel chips.

Chrome updates often. Google says Chrome releases a new update every four weeks. The version on your Mac today may not match the version in an article written last month. Treat version numbers in articles as a snapshot, not a live fact.

Release calendars disagree on the newest build. Browser Calendar lists 158.0.8127.18 for the stable Mac row dated November 4, 2026. Wikipedia lists 157.0.8103.39. WhatIsMyBrowser lists 156.0.8078.82, released November 4, 2026. Do not trust any of them for your own Mac. Open Chrome and choose Chrome > About Google Chrome. The number on that page is the one that counts.
Chrome problems people search for and how Lazur helps

Google does not publish a ranking of the questions people ask most. The closest guide is its Chrome Help Center. The home page lists 13 main topics. Several match everyday trouble: Fix problems, Change Chrome settings, Delete your history and activity, and Use AI features in Chrome. Read that list as a map of topics, not as search data.

rows: Chrome feels slow or uses a lot of memory

blocks.text: Google's official help does not cover the 'Aw, Snap' error. Third-party sites offer fixes, and they disagree. Ask Lazur to explain what the page says, then try the low-risk steps first. Close other tabs, restart Chrome, and restart your Mac if the error stays. Save your work before you restart anything.

Slow Chrome is the other common problem. Google's speed guide suggests updating Chrome, closing unused tabs, turning off extensions you do not use, and ending heavy tasks in Chrome's own Task Manager. Ask Lazur to walk you through opening Task Manager. Then ask what each column on screen means. You still end the task yourself.
Where Lazur is the wrong tool

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. If you need Chrome to fill a form or sort a long list of bookmarks, use Chrome's own tools or another method. Lazur helps you find the right control, understand it, and type text. You still do the work.

Research is a separate case. Ask Lazur to research a question. It runs the job in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension, then returns a summary and a report. Read the sources before you rely on any number. A summary is a starting point, not proof.
Privacy when an AI assistant reads your Chrome window

Privacy starts with timing. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. When you ask, the audio and a screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. Those are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did on your Mac.

In practice, a Chrome window showing a bank statement or a medical form is on screen when you hold the key. Close or move sensitive tabs before you ask. Hold the key only when you need an answer, and let go as soon as you have it.
Mistakes to avoid with an AI assistant in Chrome

items: Expecting Lazur to click. It points and guides. You click.
Asking about text that is off screen. Scroll to it first.
Trusting a version number or price from an answer without checking the source page.
Holding the key on a private page you did not mean to share with an AI provider.
Dictating a password. Store logins in Google Password Manager instead.
Mixing up the full-screen shortcut. Google lists Fn+F, while some guides give ⌘⌃F. Test both.

blocks.text: Quick start and free trial for Lazur on Mac

items: Check that your Mac runs macOS 13 Ventura or later.
Download Lazur from the [download page](/download) and open it once.
Open Chrome and load a page you use often.
Hold ⌥⌘ and ask, 'What is on this page?' Let go and listen.
Ask, 'Where is the bookmark button?' and watch for the circle.
Click into a text box, hold fn, and say one sentence.

blocks.text: Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial, and no credit card is needed. The trial starts when you first open the app. Plans and limits are on the [pricing page](/pricing), so check them there before you decide.
Start with one task you do in Chrome each day. Ask Lazur about it for a few days. Note which answers you trust and which ones you check twice. That habit tells you more than any product page can.

faq.question: Is Lazur a Chrome extension?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a Mac app. It is not a plugin or add-in for Chrome or any other app. Its research jobs run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, which use the Lazur for Chrome extension.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with Chrome on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: Which version of Chrome do I need on a Mac?
faq.answer: Google says Chrome on Mac needs macOS 13 Ventura or later. For the Chrome version itself, open Chrome > About Google Chrome. Release calendars list different newest builds, so the About page is the reliable source.

faq.question: Can Lazur click buttons in Chrome for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points at controls and guides you one click at a time, and it waits for each click. It does not click, edit files, or operate other apps for you. Dictation and drafting type text at your cursor, and you review that text before you use it.

faq.question: What shortcut reopens a tab I closed by mistake?
faq.answer: Press ⌘⇧T. Google's keyboard shortcut page lists it for reopening the tab you closed last. Keep that page open and ask Lazur to explain the list if you want the rest of the shortcuts.

faq.question: How many people use Chrome?
faq.answer: Wikipedia says Chrome has about 3.62 billion users as of March 2026, but it cites a source that the research could not read, so treat that figure with care. StatCounter puts Chrome at 66.98% of worldwide desktop browser use for October 2026. That figure covers all desktop systems, not Mac alone. No official Google total turned up in the research.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my screen to the cloud?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur keeps a memory of your requests on your Mac.

faq.question: Does Chrome have its own AI assistant?
faq.answer: Chrome includes AI features. Google's Chrome page lists Gemini in Chrome, and Google's help has a topic called Use AI features in Chrome. Lazur is a separate Mac app. It works in any app, Chrome included, and it answers out loud.

faq.question: Why does Lazur seem to miss part of a page?
faq.answer: Lazur answers from what is on screen when you hold the key. If the part you mean is scrolled out of view, scroll to it and ask again.
